                    ### Question
                    A 5-day-old male is brought to your office by his mother. The infant is experiencing bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and overall failure to thrive. A contrast enema shows a transition point at the transverse colon between dilated ascending colon and non-distended distal portion of the colon. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient's disease?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Muscle hypertrophy
opb. Mechanical bowel obstruction
opc. CFTR gene mutation
opd. Meiotic nondisjunction
ope. Failure of neural crest cell migration

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and a contrast enema showing a transition point at the transverse colon in a 5-day-old male suggests a mechanical bowel obstruction. The specific findings of a localized transition point are highly indicative of Hirschsprung disease, a condition resulting from the failure of neural crest cells to migrate during intestinal development, leading to an aganglionic segment of the colon. This aganglionic segment causes functional obstruction, aligning with the symptoms described. Evidence paths supporting the treatment of obstruction with an enema and the association of Hirschsprung disease with developmental anomalies in the colon further corroborate this diagnosis. Other options such as CFTR gene mutation, muscle hypertrophy, and meiotic nondisjunction are less likely due to the absence of their typical clinical or radiographic presentations in this scenario.
